title: Why the AI doesn't know your documents
promise: You'll understand why ChatGPT or Claude make up answers when you ask them about your own paperwork, and you'll know which of the three solutions is the one for you. By the end you'll have picked yours, with a written reason, and you won't have installed a thing.
why: Nuria runs a small accounting practice in Albacete. She has 340 files between contracts, social security circulars and emails with criteria she's set over fourteen years. She asked ChatGPT: «how many days' notice did I set for self-employed registrations?». It answered «30 calendar days», with absolute confidence. Her long-standing rule is 15. It didn't lie out of malice: it has never seen a single one of her files. She asked it something it couldn't know and it answered with what is usually true in general. That's the fault this whole block fixes.

theory.title: What it knows and what it cannot know
theory.text: A language model learned by reading an enormous amount of public text up to a certain date. In there you'll find laws, manuals, forums and millions of pages. What isn't in there, and cannot be, is anything of yours: not your contracts, not your emails, not the price spreadsheet sitting on your desktop. This isn't a limitation the paid version fixes, nor something they'll add in the next update. It's that those files have never left your computer, and nobody has seen them. The real problem, though, isn't that it doesn't know. It's that it doesn't tell you. When you ask about something it doesn't know, it doesn't go quiet and it doesn't warn you: it fills the gap with whatever is most likely. And the most likely thing, said with poise, well written and without a flicker of doubt, looks a great deal like a correct answer. That's why this is the most dangerous fault you'll meet in the whole course: it doesn't fail loudly, it fails convincingly. An error you notice is an error you fix. This one you don't notice until you've forwarded it to a client.
theory.analogy: It's a candidate who has memorized an entire library but has never set foot in your office. Ask about employment law and they'll recite it. Ask where you keep the payroll files and they'll imagine it. And they'll say both in exactly the same tone.
theory.example: Nuria asked about her registration deadline. The answer was «30 calendar days». That's the deadline that appears written down most often, so it was the most likely answer. Hers, the one she has applied since 2011 and has written in an internal circular, is 15. The difference between those two numbers is a penalty.

theory.title: Pasting it the document: the solution that works today
theory.text: The simplest way for it to know something of yours is to give it to it. You open the chat, paste the text of the contract, and now you can ask about it. It genuinely works and it solves more cases than people think, because almost everyone jumps straight to complicated setups without having tried this. It has two limits, and it's worth knowing both before you dismiss it. The first is size: every model accepts a maximum amount of text per conversation and, although these days that's a lot — hundreds of pages — 340 files won't fit. The second is memory: when you close that conversation, that's it. Tomorrow you start from zero and paste again. If what you need is to ask about one specific document, today, and you're not going to repeat it every day, this is your answer and you can skip the rest of the block with a clear conscience. Being the simple solution doesn't make it the bad one. Most projects that never get finished are projects that started on the wrong rung.
theory.analogy: It's taking the folder to your lawyer for the meeting. You don't need to set up an archive of your company in their office if you're only asking about one thing this month.
theory.example: Álvaro is a physiotherapist and once a month he receives a contract from an insurer. He pastes it into the chat, asks what changed since last year's, and he's done. He doesn't need to build anything.

theory.title: Putting it in the instructions: for what doesn't change
theory.text: The second rung is writing your own material into the assistant's fixed instructions, so it always has it in front of it without you pasting anything. That's what custom GPTs, Claude Projects or an assistant's instructions file do. It works for what is short and stable: your criteria, your way of writing, your prices, the five rules you always apply and have never written down. It stops working the moment that grows or changes often, because every change forces you to edit the instructions by hand and to remember to do it. And it takes up room: everything you put there is sent with every single question, so a very long text makes each query more expensive and, worse, distracts it from what you're actually asking. There's a point where adding more instructions makes answers worse rather than better, and it arrives sooner than you'd think. Half a page works far better than five.
theory.analogy: It's the sticky note on your monitor. Perfect for four facts you check twenty times a day. Absurd for fourteen years of filing.
theory.example: Nuria put her eleven own criteria into the instructions — the ones she knows by heart but had never written down. Half a page. That alone fixed 40% of the bad answers.

theory.title: Search before answering: that's RAG
theory.text: The third rung is the one that solves Nuria's case, and it has a technical name: RAG. The letters stand for «retrieval-augmented generation», which helps nobody understand it. In plain terms: before answering, it searches. The setup goes like this. Your 340 files are stored somewhere built for searching inside them. When you ask something, the system doesn't send your question straight to the model. First it searches your files for the four or five chunks that relate to what you asked. And then, yes, it sends the model your question with those chunks attached in front, saying: answer using this and only this. What changes isn't the model's intelligence, which is exactly the same: what changes is where the answer comes from. It no longer comes from what it remembers about the world, it comes from your paperwork. And since the system knows which chunks it used, you can ask it to tell you which file each thing came from. That's what turns an answer into something checkable, and checkable is the important word in this whole block: you're not going to stop reviewing, you're going to be able to review in ten seconds instead of ten minutes.
theory.analogy: It's the difference between asking a colleague from memory and asking them to go to the filing cabinet, pull the three folders that apply, read them, and then answer with the folders open on the desk. Same colleague. Completely different reliability.
theory.example: Nuria asks about her registration deadline. The system searches «self-employed registration deadline» in her files, finds the internal circular from 2011 and the 2019 email confirming it, passes them to the model, and the answer arrives with both references beside it. 15 days.

theory.title: What RAG doesn't fix, and it's worth knowing first
theory.text: RAG doesn't make the model infallible, and it's worth knowing that before you build it so you don't end up disappointed. It can still word a conclusion badly even when the chunks you gave it are correct, so you have to read the answer and not just trust that it came with a source. It also doesn't fix bad paperwork: if your folder has three versions of the same contract and none of them says which one governs, the system will find all three and answer with any of them, with the same confidence in all three cases. That's the most common failure of all and it isn't technical, it's about order; that's why the next lesson is entirely about tidying the paperwork. And it doesn't search the way you would: it finds by similarity of meaning, not by judgement or by calculation. If you ask «which clients owe me money?», that isn't searching, that's adding up and comparing; for that your tool is a spreadsheet or a database, not a document search. The rule that will save you weeks is this: RAG is for questions whose answer is written down somewhere. For questions whose answer has to be calculated, it isn't.
theory.analogy: It's a very fast filing clerk, not an accountant. It brings you the right folder in two seconds, but it isn't going to add up the invoices inside it.
theory.example: «What does my contract with Ferretería Beltrán say about renewals?» is a perfect question for RAG. «How much have I invoiced Ferretería Beltrán this year?» is not: that's in the accounts and it gets added up, not searched.

theory.title: How to choose, in thirty seconds
theory.text: There isn't much to think about, because the signs are clear and you can check them in a minute. If it's fewer than ten documents and you consult them now and then: paste them into the chat and get on with your life. If it's half a page of your own criteria that don't change: put it in the instructions. If it's dozens or hundreds of files, and especially if you're going to ask them things many times and you need to know where each answer comes from: RAG is your case, and the rest of the block is about building it. There's a fourth case people find hard to accept and it's worth facing head-on: if what you have is data in tables and what you want is sums, none of the three is your answer. There your tool is a spreadsheet, and the AI helps you write the formula, not guess the number. Plenty of people build an expensive document system only to end up asking it things a SUMIF would have solved.
theory.example: Nuria: 340 files, daily queries, and she needs to be able to show a client where a criterion came from. RAG, no hesitation. Álvaro: one contract a month. Paste into the chat, and build nothing.

tasks.title: Count what you actually have
tasks.action: Before deciding anything, look at what's there. Open the folder where you keep the documents you'd like to be able to query. On Windows, use the search box at the top right of the folder and sort by type; on Mac, use list view. Note three things on a piece of paper or in a note: roughly how many files there are, what types they are (PDF, Word, emails, photos of scanned paper), and how many years they span. You don't need precision: «about 300, mostly PDF and Word, since 2011» is exactly the level of detail you need.
tasks.expect: Three facts written down. If on opening the folder you realise it's twelve files and not three hundred, you've just saved yourself the whole block: your solution is to paste them into the chat.
tasks.stuck: If they're spread across five different places (the computer, Drive, email, an external disk and WhatsApp), don't move them yet. Write down the five places. That's information in itself: it tells you that before building anything you have a gathering job to do, and that job is the longest part of the whole block.

tasks.title: See it make things up with your own eyes
tasks.where: In ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini, in a new chat
tasks.action: This is much easier to understand by seeing it than by reading about it. Think of a fact that only exists in your documents: a rule of yours, a clause you negotiated, a price you only apply to one client. Open a new chat, without pasting anything, and ask about that fact directly, as if it knew. Pay attention to the tone of the answer, not just the content.
tasks.prompt:
I work in [YOUR SECTOR]. I need you to confirm a specific fact about my own operation: [THE QUESTION, exactly as you'd ask a colleague in your office].

Answer in two parts, in this order and without skipping either:
1. Your answer to the question.
2. Where exactly you got that fact: whether it's from a document of mine you've seen, or it's what's usual in the sector, or you're imagining it. Be literal, don't soften it.
tasks.expect: In part 1 it gives you an answer that sounds right. In part 2 it admits it hasn't seen any document of yours. Save that answer or screenshot it: it's the reason this block exists, and when you're three lessons in and wrestling with an installation it'll remind you what you're doing it for.
tasks.stuck: If in part 1 it refuses to answer and says outright that it can't know, congratulations: you got a cautious model. Push with «give me your best estimate anyway» and you'll see the invented fact appear. That's the default behaviour as soon as the question is slightly less obvious.

tasks.title: Write down your own criteria
tasks.where: In a text file or a note
tasks.action: This task is worth doing on its own, whatever you choose afterwards. Almost everyone has between five and fifteen rules of their own that they know by heart and have never written down: deadlines they apply, exceptions they make, how they charge, things they won't accept. Write them out. One per line, no flourishes, the way you'd tell someone starting work with you tomorrow. Date the file. If it takes you more than twenty minutes, you're padding: cut.
tasks.expect: Between five and fifteen lines. Half a page at most. If you end up with forty, check whether they're really criteria or you're describing processes: processes go somewhere else.
tasks.stuck: If you go blank, get at it through irritation: think of the last three times you corrected someone because they did something wrong. Behind every correction there's an unwritten rule of yours. Another way in: look at the last ten emails you sent explaining something.

tasks.title: Put your criteria where the assistant always sees them
tasks.action: Now you're going to try the second rung, which takes four minutes to set up and already gives you a result. In ChatGPT, left menu, Projects button, and create a new one named after your work. Inside you'll see an instructions field. In Claude it's the same: Projects, new one, and the field is called «Custom instructions». Paste in the criteria from the previous task, preceded by a line saying: «These are my working criteria. When you answer something that depends on one of them, apply it and tell me which one you applied.» Save, and ask it the same question as task 2 inside that project.
tasks.expect: Now it answers with your criterion, not the generic one, and tells you which one it used. With half a page of text you've just fixed part of the problem without installing anything. Notice which questions still fail: those are exactly the ones that need the full documents.
tasks.stuck: If you can't find Projects, your plan doesn't include them. Never mind: paste the criteria at the start of each conversation. It's more tedious but it works the same. And if it answers with the generic criterion even though it has yours written down, say «according to my criteria» in the question and you'll see it pick them up.

tasks.title: Decide which case is yours, and write it down
tasks.where: In the same note where you wrote the three facts
tasks.action: With what you've seen in the four previous tasks, you have everything you need to decide. Write a single sentence in this format: «My case is [paste in the chat / fixed instructions / RAG] because [the reason, with your numbers].» The reason has to carry a figure of yours, not an impression. If you're torn between two, take the simpler of the two: you can always move up a rung, and moving down hurts more.
tasks.expect: One sentence, with a number in it. For example: «My case is RAG because it's 340 files spanning fourteen years and I consult several every day.» Or: «My case is pasting into the chat because it's nine documents and I look at them once a month.»
tasks.stuck: If you wrote RAG but you have fewer than thirty files, stop and reread the theory. Building RAG for thirty documents means spending two afternoons on something that pasting text solves. If you wrote RAG and it's hundreds, carry on to lesson 31: that's where the document preparation starts, and that's where this is really won or lost.

tasks.title: Measure how much time you lose searching
tasks.action: You'll need this number in block 10, when you have to justify the project, and along the way it tells you whether it's worth building at all. For three days, every time you go looking for something in your documents, note two things: what you were looking for and how many minutes it took. You don't need a stopwatch, «about 5» is fine. If some day you search for nothing, note that too: the zeros are part of the data.
tasks.expect: Between ten and thirty lines after three days, and a total in minutes. What's normal in a job with paperwork is twenty to forty minutes a day, which is several hours a month. If you get two minutes over three days, you have your answer: don't build anything.
tasks.stuck: If you keep forgetting to write it down, stick a note on your screen for the three days. And if you feel like you're exaggerating the time, don't revise it down: count the time spent deciding which folder to look in and the time reopening the file you'd already closed.

tasks.title: Check whether your question is searched or calculated
tasks.action: Take the questions you noted in the previous task and sort them into two columns. In the first, the ones answered by reading a paragraph written somewhere: «what did I agree with this client?», «what was my rule for this?». In the second, the ones answered by adding, counting or comparing figures across documents: «how much have I invoiced?», «how many active clients do I have?». Count how many are in each.
tasks.expect: Two columns with numbers. If the first is clearly longer, RAG is your tool. If the second wins, what you need is to tidy your data into a spreadsheet, and this block will be of little use to you.
tasks.stuck: If a question feels like both, split it: «what discount do I apply to this client and how much have I invoiced them?» is two questions, one from each column, and each has its own tool.

tasks.title: Test the chat's limit with your own documents
tasks.action: Before dismissing the simple solution, measure how far it goes. Take the three or four documents you consult most and paste them all into one conversation, one after another. Then ask two or three real questions from the ones you noted. Watch whether it warns you that it's too much text, and whether the answers hold up towards the end of the conversation.
tasks.expect: Almost certainly they fit and it answers well. Right there you've discovered the real size of your problem: if your frequent queries concentrate on five documents, you don't need to build anything even if you have three hundred stored.
tasks.stuck: If it tells you the text is too long, remove one and repeat. The number of documents it accepts at once is a useful figure: it's how many you can consult without building anything. And if the answers get worse as the conversation goes on, that's the sign it's running out of room: start another.

matters: That a model has never seen a single one of your files, and will answer about them anyway.
That there are three solutions of different sizes, and most people pick the biggest without needing it.
That RAG means searching your documents before answering, and the valuable part is being able to see where each answer came from.
That if your question is answered by calculating rather than reading, none of the three is your tool.
ignore: What an embedding is and how it's calculated. You'll use it without knowing, the same way you use wifi.
Which vector database is best. Every one you'll meet in this course will do to start.
The accuracy percentages in the articles. They're measured on other people's documents, not yours.
canDo: Explain why it gave you a false fact with total confidence.
Choose between the three solutions with a reason and a figure.
Have your criteria written down for the first time.
Make the assistant apply your criteria instead of the generic ones.
cantDo: Query your full documents yet: that starts in the next lesson.
Get it to cite the file each fact comes from.
Ask about data that has to be added up or compared.
Trust an answer without reading it, not even with RAG in place.
words: Searching your documents before answering, and answering with what was found. The letters stand for «retrieval-augmented generation».
When it invents a fact and presents it with the same confidence as a true one. It isn't a rare error: it's the default when it doesn't know something.
How much text fits in one conversation. When it fills up, the first thing you said stops being there.
Fixed text the assistant has in front of it on every question, without you pasting it each time.
The place where your documents are stored, prepared to be searched by meaning rather than by exact word.
Having the answer say which file and which part each thing came from. It's what makes it checkable.
next: You know RAG is your case and why. In lesson 31 the real work starts, and it isn't the work people expect: before building any tool you have to prepare the documents. That's where this either works or hands you half-answers, and almost everyone who fails, fails at this step.
